chapters.title: Lakehouse, OneLake, and access layers
points: Files can preserve raw structured, semi-structured, and binary artifacts. Tables provide a Delta-aware analytical representation; an uploaded CSV is not automatically a SQL table.
OneLake is the tenant-wide storage foundation, built on ADLS technology. A lakehouse is one Fabric item using it. Bronze, silver, and gold describe processing stages, not separate storage products.
Spark, SQL analytics, OneLake storage APIs, REST management, and Power BI consumption are different surfaces. Match permissions, protocol, and supported operations to the intended task.
chapters.caveat: The video's blanket capacity-access statement is simplified. Current OneLake documentation distinguishes direct paused-capacity transactions from reads through a shortcut on an active consumer capacity.

chapters.title: Internal/external shortcuts and caching
points: A plain shortcut references existing files or tables across workspaces or supported external systems, instead of creating another independently managed dataset copy.

Internal shortcuts can share Files and Delta Tables. External sources include ADLS, S3, S3-compatible storage, GCS, Dataverse, and supported Iceberg integrations; format and placement still determine consumption.

Workspace caching serves eligible external reads from cached content, reducing repeat remote requests. Documented inactivity retention is 1–28 days, reset by access; source-version checks refresh updated content. Files greater than 1 GB are excluded.
chapters.caveat: Supported shortcut sources and supported cache sources are different lists. Cache currently includes GCS, S3, S3-compatible, and on-premises gateway shortcuts. A shortcut remains a source dependency, not a backup.

chapters.title: Delta files, transaction logs, and controlled changes
points: Delta adds transaction metadata to columnar Parquet data. The committed log defines which files comprise a snapshot, rather than every physical file being current data.

Appends write files and publish a transaction. Updates/deletes/merges can leave historical physical files even when the latest snapshot no longer includes their rows. ACID preserves consistency; optimistic write conflicts can still occur.
Time travel reads earlier snapshots while schema evolution permits controlled structural changes. Neither is a promise to keep unlimited history or silently accept every incoming schema.
chapters.caveat: The video's delete illustration describes copy-on-write. Deletion vectors can represent removed rows without immediately rewriting the original Parquet file. Schema evolution is opt-in; default schema enforcement is protective.

chapters.title: VACUUM, OPTIMIZE, and V-Order have different goals
points: VACUUM physically removes eligible obsolete data files outside the retention threshold. Its main goal is storage cleanup. It does not compact active files, reconstruct deleted historical data, or delete the Delta log as its ordinary purpose.
OPTIMIZE compacts active small files. V-Order optimizes Parquet layout at writing or rewriting time for read-heavy consumption, with workload-dependent write overhead.

Recovery requires sufficient retained logs AND files. Inspect cleanup candidates and concurrent-reader requirements before deletion; a seven-day retention setting is not a guaranteed seven-day recovery SLA.
chapters.caveat: V-Order is no longer enabled by default for all new workspaces. Check session, table, and write-level settings. The cited roughly 15% write overhead is an average observation, not a universal guarantee.

chapters.title: Partition hierarchy, pruning, and cardinality
points: Hive-style partitioning places data into directories for populated value combinations of one or more keys. The logical row set is unchanged.
Usable predicates on partition keys can skip directories. A key with many distinct values, or too many combined keys, can create tiny partitions and frequent small-file writes.
Estimate volume per populated partition and align the layout with real predicates or writer boundaries. A tiny teaching table is intentionally unsuitable as a production partitioning example.
chapters.caveat: Current Fabric guidance emphasizes partitioning for disjoint concurrent writers and considers liquid clustering for many read-performance goals. The lab's Hive-style questions explicitly state the selected strategy.

chapters.title: OneLake file explorer: safe abstraction boundaries
points: The Windows-integrated file tool is useful for managing supported raw artifacts in Files, including uploaded reference files.
A Delta directory is not a set of independent documents to edit. Mutating active Parquet or _delta_log content outside Delta-aware operations can break transactional consistency.
Use authorized Spark/Delta writes for row changes and the supported lifecycle operations for deletion. Do not copy the video's casual folder-deletion suggestion into a production runbook.
chapters.caveat: File-management convenience does not remove governance, transaction, or dependency requirements.

chapters.title: Demo: raw uploads and lakehouse schemas
points: The demo uploads a text file and a CSV to a Files subfolder, showing that raw-format preservation is separate from creating analytical Delta tables.
The Tables area contains the default dbo schema and a custom schema in a schema-enabled lakehouse. Schemas organize names; they are not partition keys or medallion stages.
Use qualified table names when saving or querying. Renaming or moving a table requires updating dependent Notebook, dataflow, and SQL references.
chapters.caveat: Schema support is currently enabled by default in portal creation but must be explicitly requested through the creation REST API. Existing non-schema lakehouses remain a distinct case.

chapters.title: Demo: one logical dataset, three physical layouts
points: The notebook creates an unpartitioned table, a category-partitioned table, and a category-region-partitioned table with the same sample rows.
Switching to file view reveals Parquet files, _delta_log, and the partition-folder hierarchy. This is inspection of physical organization, not proof that one design is fastest.
Combined partition columns multiply populated combinations. Compare candidate layouts on representative workloads and distributions rather than copying the demo's folder count.
chapters.caveat: The presenter explicitly uses the small dataset to illustrate the mechanism, not to recommend partitioning it.

chapters.title: Demo: portal maintenance and scheduled automation
points: The Maintenance action exposes compaction, optional V-Order, and VACUUM for Delta tables. The same underlying goals can be implemented using code.
Thousands of tables call for a scheduled, observable maintenance workflow, not a manual click loop. Run maintenance with success dependencies after ingestion and respect per-table retention needs.
Spark notebook commands and management APIs are distinct from the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint; do not paste Spark maintenance SQL into its T-SQL editor.
chapters.caveat: The dedicated Pipeline Lakehouse Maintenance activity is currently Preview. The lab uses a generally applicable Notebook-and-Pipeline pattern rather than assuming preview availability.

chapters.title: Demo: schema shortcut and Files shortcut
points: A new schema-enabled consumer lakehouse references the producer schema. The icon signals a shortcut, and the visible tables still reference producer data.
A second shortcut references a producer Files folder containing the two raw files. No transformations are selected in that demo.
The same reference concept extends to supported external stores, but source format, credentials, placement, and feature-specific behavior remain important.
chapters.caveat: A Files shortcut with no transformation is not a Delta table. Shortcut transformations are a separate modern feature and may change the no-materialization assumptions.

chapters.title: Demo: SQL analytics, SSMS, read-only data, and views
points: The lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint exposes synchronized Delta tables through T-SQL, including suitable shortcut tables. SSMS can connect through its SQL/TDS connection information.
The demo contrasts successful SELECT with rejected UPDATE against underlying lakehouse data. Spark is the appropriate engineering surface for those Delta writes.
CREATE VIEW succeeds because it creates an endpoint SQL object. That view is not a newly materialized managed Delta table visible as the same object to Spark.
chapters.caveat: Read-only data does not mean no SQL metadata operations. Supported read views, functions, and stored procedures can exist within the endpoint boundary.

chapters.title: Demo: retrieve the correct connection information
points: The item settings expose SQL connection information for SQL clients. A storage path and a SQL server endpoint are not interchangeable.
OneLake supports ADLS/Blob-compatible access and ABFSS addressing for storage-aware clients. REST management actions and semantic-model consumption use their own contracts.
Confirm identity, permissions, and supported operations for the surface used; possession of a URI is not authorization.
chapters.caveat: The lab analyzes the complete available auto-generated transcript and the narrated demonstrations. It does not claim pixel-by-pixel inspection of on-screen content absent from that transcript.

chapters.title: Warehouse architecture and workload selection
points: Warehouse presents a relational SQL experience over Delta/Parquet data in OneLake. The video's usual silver/gold placement is a pattern, not a mandatory medallion mapping.
The raw-artifact and Spark workflow belongs on a suitable engineering surface. Curated relational processing and transactional T-SQL requirements guide the Warehouse choice.
chapters.caveat: Familiar SQL Server concepts do not guarantee feature parity. Review current SQL support rather than importing triggers and other objects unchanged.

chapters.title: Schemas, tables, views, functions, and procedures
points: Schemas group named objects. Tables hold rows; ordinary views save read logic; functions return values or composable rows; procedures execute workflows and can return result sets.
Choose the object's contract before deciding where to reuse it. A procedure result set is not invoked as a table expression in FROM.
chapters.caveat: The endpoint supports SQL read objects, but that does not authorize writes to its underlying Lakehouse Delta tables.

chapters.title: Pipelines, Dataflow Gen2, notebooks, and connectors
points: The video lists Pipeline copies, Power Query transformations with Dataflow Gen2, T-SQL notebooks, Spark Warehouse loading, cross-database SQL, COPY INTO, Copy Jobs, and external clients.
Treat preparation, movement, orchestration, and execution target as separate decisions. Documented notebook steps can run against the primary Warehouse; success dependencies coordinate validation.
chapters.caveat: Native Spark connector writes depend on Runtime 2.0. Its authentication contract differs from a generic Entra-capable SQL driver. The video's judgment that some tools are beyond exam scope is not a current syllabus guarantee.

chapters.title: Reading data through SQL, Power BI, and clients
points: SELECT, joins, filters, and saved read logic serve SQL clients and downstream analytics. Notebook, Pipeline, and Dataflow integrations are alternative clients, not new grants.
Retrieve the actual SQL connection string for TDS clients; OneLake file paths belong to a different interface.
chapters.caveat: Use supported Entra authentication and authorized access. A server name, driver, or UI attachment does not grant access to every item.

chapters.title: Historical states and reporting cutoffs
points: Time travel supports comparisons and reproducible reads while ingestion continues. It can reveal retained states before inserts, deletes, or truncation.
A stable report needs the intended shared UTC cutoff, sufficient available history, and ordinary query authorization.
chapters.caveat: The video says 30 days is fixed. Current Warehouse documentation allows 1–120 whole calendar days, with a 30-day default. Retention is not a complete backup or disaster-recovery plan.

chapters.title: Clones: shared initial files, independent table state
points: A zero-copy table clone initially references existing data files through copied metadata. It provides a candidate for testing or comparison without an immediate full data-file copy.
New changes can cause source and clone storage to diverge. Initial zero-copy does not mean unlimited future storage is free.
chapters.caveat: Current documentation supports table clones within one Warehouse, including different schemas; it does not support cross-Warehouse or cross-workspace table clones. Security inheritance described in the video is supported; test effective privileges.

chapters.title: Visual query explanation and narrated canvas demo
points: The presenter joins person and address data on the visual canvas, inspects generated SQL, and saves a view or exports query logic.
A canvas join can still multiply parent rows or discard unmatched parents. Review join grain, deterministic child-row selection, and null behavior.
chapters.caveat: Promotional content at 7:37–8:13 contains no assessed Fabric concepts. Saving an ordinary view does not independently store its result set.

chapters.title: SQL templates, Copilot, and SSMS connection
points: The narrated SQL editor demo shows query and object templates plus assisted authoring. SSMS exposes the same authorized SQL objects through the connection string from item settings.
The Lakehouse SQL data surface is contrasted with Warehouse writes. Changing client applications does not change the engine's supported operations.
chapters.caveat: Assisted SQL still requires review. The complete available auto-caption transcript was analyzed; exact unseen UI settings and on-screen SQL are not asserted as independently inspected.

chapters.title: Employee table and a query-time tenure view
points: The demo creates a schema, an employee table, and six starting rows, then a view that derives years employed and seniority.
A current-time expression evaluates at query time. Historical input rows alone do not specify a complete business reporting clock; use an explicit as-of date when reproducibility matters.
chapters.caveat: DATEDIFF(year) counts year boundaries, not completed hire anniversaries. The lab's original date exercise supplies explicit dates; it does not claim to transcribe the demo's unseen expression.

chapters.title: Parameterized employee procedure and optional department
points: The narrated procedure filters employee seniority and uses an optional department parameter. Its examples contrast unrestricted departments with a specified department.
The harder exercises specify exact input rows, NULL cases, and boolean grouping so the required result can be derived without guessing.
chapters.caveat: Test IS NULL explicitly. COALESCE-to-the-same-column can silently drop rows whose column value is NULL. Use an inline TVF when a composable parameterized read is required.

chapters.title: COPY INTO: private CSV, header, permissions, and retry
points: The source CSV contributes three employees to the six-row table. COPY settings identify the file format and header handling.
Source authorization and target SQL authorization are separate. A repeated append must be made safe by the load design if a lost acknowledgement can trigger replay.
chapters.caveat: Default source access uses the executing Entra identity. Blob data-plane read differs from management-plane access. The lab also adds the current Workspace Identity credential mode as an explicitly marked extension.

chapters.title: Time-travel demo: six rows before the three-row load
points: The demonstrated earlier snapshot returns six employees, compared with nine after the CSV load. The historical SELECT uses a statement-level UTC timestamp.
Selected columns, view creation time, and actual available data matter when reproducing a historical report. Current schema constraints do not equal historical schema reconstruction.
chapters.caveat: Current Lakehouse endpoint time travel is conditional Preview support: New metadata sync must be enabled at endpoint creation, and table-level vacuum retention limits history. The Warehouse retention setting does not apply to it. Promotion at 19:49–20:29 is unassessed.

chapters.title: Cross-database demo and one-way SQL materialization
points: The presenter creates a two-row Lakehouse employee Delta table, adds the SQL endpoint to Warehouse Object Explorer, combines rows using three-part names, and inserts the two source rows into Warehouse.
The narrated totals progress from Warehouse nine plus Lakehouse two to Warehouse eleven. An added Source literal identifies origin and can affect UNION duplicate comparison.
chapters.caveat: The demonstrated route is in one workspace. Reverse INSERT through the Lakehouse SQL endpoint is unsupported. The lab's duplicate-row exercise is original and supplies its full SQL rather than inferring unseen demo code.

chapters.title: Clone demo: insert, truncate, recover, and clone a prior state
points: A clone begins with eleven rows. A later source insert produces twelve source rows while the clone stays at eleven; source truncation leaves the clone available.
Repopulating from that clone restores eleven rows and omits the later insert. The presenter also demonstrates a historical clone timestamp; the outro adds no assessed concepts.
chapters.caveat: The recovery exercises require unchanged schema, retained history, permissions, validation, and an explicit production-change checkpoint. This lab simulates decisions; it does not execute live Fabric recovery.

chapters.title: Source scope and exam alignment
points: This is episode 7 of a DP-700 series, not a complete DP-600 course. The creator positions it as pipeline fundamentals, followed by demos and two introductory practice items.
The DP-600 connection is analytical data ingestion/preparation and maintaining analytics assets. Detailed orchestration/replay exercises in this pack are explicitly identified extensions.
chapters.caveat: The published DP-600 guide is headed 'Skills measured as of October 19, 2026', later than this lab's October 10 review. Its change log marks Prepare data unchanged. This pack does not claim full current or upcoming exam coverage.

chapters.title: Movement, orchestration, and transformation
points: The canvas combines activities and their dependencies. Pipelines can invoke notebooks, Dataflow Gen2, and supported external services.
The video's main distinction is movement/orchestration versus complex preparation. The lab extends this into workload selection and quality-gated release.
chapters.caveat: Classifying Copy under more than one activity category does not expand its transformation contract. Choose an engine by the actual operation, not a category label.

chapters.title: Activity families and nested workflows
points: The presenter surveys movement, transformation, and control activities, including loops, conditions, variables, SQL, notebook/dataflow execution, and nested pipelines.
The original examples here make activity inputs and a successful completion barrier explicit rather than assuming same-named inputs propagate automatically.
chapters.caveat: The video's claim that Copy is the only movement activity reflects its date. The current overview also lists Copy job. Pipeline activities and deployment pipelines are different concepts.

chapters.title: Connections, gateways, and directional support
points: External services require an appropriate connection and supported authentication; some require a gateway. Support varies by source/destination direction and activity.
Read the connector matrix before choosing a route. The SQL Server question provides its matrix premise rather than assuming all database connectors behave alike.
chapters.caveat: Gateway connectivity does not grant database permissions. Fabric's on-premises gateway should not be replaced conceptually with an ADF integration runtime.

chapters.title: Parameters, variables, expressions, and child inputs
points: Parameters bring run inputs into a reusable workflow and can be passed from a parent to a child. Variables represent internal execution state; defaults and Set Variable are introduced.
Dynamic expressions can compose values such as file paths. Harder extensions add typed expressions, array output shapes, per-item inputs, and execution versus business identity.
chapters.caveat: Detailed parallel-isolation and replay contracts are lab extensions, not claims that the video demonstrates them. Never assume shared mutable state is an iteration-local input.

chapters.title: Schedules, time zones, triggers, and monitoring
points: The theory describes schedule activation, recurrence, start/end dates, and time zones. Event triggers and Monitoring hub are mentioned but deferred to other episodes.
The lab distinguishes initiation from readiness: arrival can start a run, while success/quality dependencies determine release.
chapters.caveat: The current docs add multiple schedules, explicit scheduled parameter values, event-derived inputs, and Preview scheduling features. Preview extensions are not treated as mandatory exam facts here.

chapters.title: Demo setup: artifact, templates, sample data, assistant
points: After a short channel-support segment, the demo uploads movies.csv to a new folder in Lakehouse Files, creates a data pipeline, and selects a blank canvas.
The presenter explains templates, sample-data practice, and Copy assistant as authoring accelerators, then uses Copy data directly.
chapters.caveat: Uploading a CSV to Files does not itself create a Delta table. Templates and assistants reduce setup work; they do not prove a batch's business correctness.

chapters.title: Canvas dependencies, Wait, schedule UI, and JSON
points: The presenter adds a Wait after Copy, explores recurrence settings and storage-event initiation, and opens the underlying pipeline JSON.
The lab tests the difference between a delay and a success dependency, and between versioned definitions and runtime outcomes.
chapters.caveat: The visual canvas writes configuration; a successful source commit does not prove the corresponding pipeline ran. ADF deployment assumptions must not be imported wholesale.

chapters.title: General policy and parsed Files source
points: The demo points out timeout, retries, retry interval, and secure input/output. It selects the Lakehouse Files source and changes Binary to Delimited text.
Preview shows the CSV interpreted as rows with a header. The harder parser problem supplies a quoted delimiter rather than assuming every input matches the demo defaults.
chapters.caveat: General UI and REST descriptions show differing defaults; the questions supply explicit policy values. Secure input/output changes logging, not parsing or data validation.

chapters.title: Delta destination, replacement, mapping, and parallel copy
points: The demo targets a Lakehouse table, chooses Overwrite, imports mappings, changes year to integer and rating to double, and explains dropping/renaming mapped columns.
It briefly points out copy parallelism and optimization settings. The lab adds distinct snapshot/incremental contracts and a numeric bottleneck problem.
chapters.caveat: Current Lakehouse configuration also documents Upsert; the video's small example is not an exhaustive write-action list. Joins and aggregates need an appropriate preparation engine.

chapters.title: Execution, metrics, and table verification
points: Copy succeeds before Wait, according to the success dependency. The presenter inspects Copy execution details and refreshes the Lakehouse to inspect the new table and types.
The lab extends transport verification into row reconciliation and explicit business validation before release.
chapters.caveat: A Succeeded run is evidence of activity execution, not a guarantee that uniqueness, referential completeness, or financial rules passed.

chapters.title: Parameterize source and destination
points: The demo creates file_name and table_name parameters, shows a variable default, and selects dynamic content for the file and target table.
A new table name produces movies2; inspecting activity input shows the resolved value. Typed expression and notebook binding questions go beyond this basic example.
chapters.caveat: Parameters stay fixed during a run. Defaults are fallback values, not a rule that callers cannot provide values. Interpolation returns text; whole-field expressions can retain numeric types.

chapters.title: Success, failure, skipped, and completion traces
points: The Wait-chain demo shows a success path, a failure-only branch that does not run, a skip-dependent successor, and a Completion dependency.
The essential distinction is that Completion covers success or failure, while a skipped predecessor requires the skip condition.
chapters.caveat: Follow the immediate predecessor at each edge. A downstream skipped activity is not a failed activity, and a fixed Wait is not a readiness check.

chapters.title: Inactive activities and the old configuration workaround
points: The presenter deactivates Copy and demonstrates how its assigned status affects downstream branching without performing the transfer.
The video changes outgoing dependencies to influence the inactive marker. Current authoring provides a direct Mark activity as selection under General.
chapters.caveat: Explicitly choose Succeeded, Failed, or Skipped in the current UI and save changes. An inactive placeholder has no normal Copy output fields; assigned success does not show that data was copied.

chapters.title: Creator practice items, worked reasoning, and outro
points: After a brief practice-site promotion, the first introductory example combines an inactive success-marked Wait with a failure-only successor; neither performs work.
The second contrasts on-premises/cloud movement, limited transformation, and parallelism. Our new scenarios change constraints and require more reasoning instead of reproducing those items.
chapters.caveat: The complete auto-caption transcript was analyzed. It is not a frame-by-frame inspection; diagram details are derived only where the narration states them. Original question wording is not copied.

chapters.title: Three original cases: publication, replay, and promotion
points: Retail separates raw evidence, current snapshot, quality gates, and duplicate delivery. Finance supplies a stable watermark interval and an explicit atomic publication mechanism. Alpine tests parallel entity inputs and environment bindings.

These are original advanced practice cases, supported by current docs and explicitly stated engineering assumptions. They add application, failure analysis, code interpretation, and constrained choices.
chapters.caveat: The 100-minute timer and exact-match scoring are this lab's training settings. Microsoft does not publish a live DP-600 item bank or guarantee a particular question-type mix; this is not a calibrated reproduction.

chapters.title: Episode scope and the DP-600 connection
points: Episode 14 of the creator's DP-700 series introduces modeling, keys, facts/dimensions, star/snowflake, and SCD types 0–3, then narrates Warehouse demonstrations.
For DP-600, the useful connection is implementing star schemas, denormalization, joins, data quality, and semantic relationships. Advanced loader/replay cases here extend that foundation.
chapters.caveat: The published DP-600 guide is headed October 19, 2026, after this October 10 review; its change log shows Prepare data unchanged. This topic pack is not a full-syllabus claim or a reproduction of secure exam items.

chapters.title: Why modeling matters: structure and trustworthy totals
points: The video starts from messy heterogeneous data and explains structure, relationships, consistency, performance, and scalability as modeling goals.
The lab adds a concrete grain decision: repeated order headers must not become additive line measures. Numeric identifiers also remain identifiers.
chapters.caveat: A schema does not itself guarantee correct data. In Fabric Warehouse, declared PK/UNIQUE/FK constraints are unenforced, so duplicates and invalid references require explicit checks.

chapters.title: Customers, orders, and key semantics
points: The customer/order blueprint introduces a primary key as an identifier and a foreign key as a relationship reference. Repeated customer attributes motivate separation.
Historical dimensions add a second identity level: CustomerId names an entity, while CustomerSK identifies one stored version. Facts must retain the intended version reference.
chapters.caveat: A declared key is not evidence that the actual values are unique. A natural-key SQL join against several versions can multiply facts even when each surrogate is unique.

chapters.title: Separate event rows from descriptive entities
points: The example separates orders from customer descriptions instead of repeating all descriptions in the order table.
Preparation should also state whether a row is an order, a line, or another observation before aggregation. A transaction rate must be interpreted with its matching quantity.
chapters.caveat: Do not confuse denormalizing a dimension hierarchy with repeating every descriptive attribute or header measure on every fact row.

chapters.title: Facts, dimensions, and analytical meaning
points: Facts carry observations and measurements; dimensions describe entities used to interpret those events. Fact keys connect the two.
The lab distinguishes a current list-price attribute from captured transaction price, and separates second-level price observations from slowly changing customer attributes.
chapters.caveat: The video's relative table sizes are typical, not a rule for classification. Meaning and grain determine the design, and an integer key is not automatically a measure.

chapters.title: Star versus snowflake: reporting tradeoffs
points: A star connects a fact to flat dimensions; a snowflake normalizes a dimension into additional related tables. The video compares join count and repeated descriptive storage.
A combined product hierarchy can be easier for authors to navigate. The lab's constrained choice specifies the required single-table hierarchy rather than promising universal performance.
chapters.caveat: The suggestion that snowflake is inherently better for changing data is too broad. SCD2 also works in a star; topology does not automatically create history, and performance depends on the actual workload.

chapters.title: SCD0: deliberately retain the approved value
points: The presenter uses an unchanged value policy and mentions date-of-birth and calendar examples.
Our scenario makes immutability an explicit business rule and routes exceptions through an audit process.
chapters.caveat: A birth date or calendar field is not intrinsically immune to data-entry errors. The normal load's immutable policy and an authorized correction process must be distinguished.

chapters.title: SCD1: current state and corrections
points: The example replaces a customer's country rather than retaining a prior row. This supports a current-state interpretation.
The lab tests historical reclassification after overwrite and an explicitly global email correction across retained versions. Fact amounts can stay unchanged while their region grouping changes.
chapters.caveat: Type 1 is useful for corrections and current-state attributes; saying it generally fails real-world needs is too sweeping. A full current-only refresh cannot invent discarded versions.

chapters.title: SCD2: version identities and effective intervals
points: A country change expires the old customer version and inserts a new version. Natural identity repeats, while the surrogate identity changes. Dates and an optional current flag describe validity.
The advanced questions require one justified event-time match, retained persistent keys, and complete historical evidence. Inferred-member completion is explicitly separated from a real change.
chapters.caveat: This lab adopts [ValidFrom, ValidTo) UTC intervals. That precise boundary contract is an extension. A current flag is convenient metadata, not a replacement for a valid chain or an automatic way to recover old values.

chapters.title: SCD3: current and one previous value
points: The presenter introduces extra attributes for limited history rather than adding a version row for each change.
The examples trace repeated roll-forward updates and compare the resulting one-row summary with a three-version history.
chapters.caveat: Keeping one previous value does not retain an unrestricted timeline. Additional SCD variants mentioned by the creator are outside this video's teaching scope.

chapters.title: Promotion, Warehouse setup, and write engines
points: After a brief promotion, the demo creates a schema and tables in a Warehouse, using T-SQL. The creator notes Lakehouse Spark SQL/PySpark as alternative implementation routes; type 0 has no changing-row demo.
The lab tests choosing a supported writer when applying the same conceptual pattern to a Lakehouse.
chapters.caveat: Warehouse DML support must not be assumed for the Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint. Narrated setup is not a complete production loader or proof that uniqueness is enforced.

chapters.title: Warehouse SCD1 demonstration: product price overwrite
points: The product example begins with a laptop and headphones, then increases the laptop price by 100. The existing row is updated, with no retained old price in that dimension.
The quiz adds discount and quantity constraints to test whether an actual-sale measure should use captured fact economics or a dimension's current list price.
chapters.caveat: An updated product attribute does not automatically rewrite a transaction price already stored in facts. Decide what historical report semantics require.

chapters.title: Warehouse SCD2 demonstration: table structure
points: The next table includes a surrogate, product identity, descriptive fields, start/end validity, and current status. Initially two products each have one version.
A far-future end or a null end is a modeling choice. The lab explicitly states the representation before asking for its temporal predicate.
chapters.caveat: Keep end representation, interval bounds, and current flags consistent. Surrogate generation must preserve existing fact references; regenerating keys from today's data can invalidate them.

chapters.title: Warehouse SCD2 demonstration: expire and replace
points: The narrated operation sets the laptop's old end and current status, then inserts its new price with a different surrogate. The business product identity remains the same.
The production extensions stage canonical changes before mutation, group writes atomically, detect null transitions, reconcile replays, and check the final chain.
chapters.caveat: The demonstration does not specify a complete concurrency, failure, or duplicate-source contract. Our loader case supplies those assumptions expressly. Exact on-screen SQL was not independently frame-inspected.

chapters.title: Warehouse SCD3 demonstration: roll current into previous
points: The final table has current and previous price attributes and a current-value start timestamp. It starts with current prices and null previous prices.
When a price changes, the old current price is retained as previous and the new current price replaces it; the operation updates the row instead of inserting a history version.
chapters.caveat: A timestamp on the latest value and one previous column cannot answer every earlier as-of question after repeated changes. Do not infer a full chain from this summary.

chapters.title: Creator practice, original cases, and research limits
points: The closing practice contrasts current/previous-only history with complete versioned address history. Promotion and outro are recognized but add no separate assessed skill.
Our regional-sales, product-pricing, and dimension-loader cases are new scenarios with constrained decisions, code interpretation, boundary reasoning, and independently calculated totals.
chapters.caveat: Analysis uses the complete English auto-caption transcript and narrated demonstrations, not a frame-by-frame visual inspection. The creator's question wording is not copied. This 40-question, 100-minute challenge has lab exact-match scoring, with no official scaled score or calibrated live-exam difficulty claim.

chapters.title: Episode scope and exam alignment
points: Episode 15 introduces the remaining Eventhouse data store, followed by theory, narrated Fabric demonstrations, and two introductory practice items.

The DP-600 guide explicitly includes OneLake integration for Eventhouse, analytical store selection, and KQL selection/filtering/aggregation. Detailed materialized-view administration and lifecycle scenarios here are marked as extensions.
chapters.caveat: The published DP-600 guide is headed October 19, 2026, later than this October 10 review; its change log marks Prepare data unchanged and Query and analyze data as a minor change. This topic pack does not claim full exam coverage or calibrated live-exam difficulty.

chapters.title: Eventhouse, KQL databases, and cross-engine access
points: The video describes fast event ingestion and analysis for telemetry, clickstreams, and IoT data. Eventhouse contains KQL databases and offers several ingestion routes.
KQL is the main analytical language. OneLake availability exposes a Delta representation for other supported Fabric engines, while retaining the KQL analytical store.
chapters.caveat: Eventhouse also manages shared resources and monitoring; treating it merely as an inert folder understates its role. Familiar SQL syntax does not imply a complete transactional SQL engine or identical support across all Fabric stores.

chapters.title: Workload strengths and measurable requirements
points: The narrated examples are high-rate event ingestion, semistructured logs, operational dashboards, and anomaly analysis while data continues to arrive.
The scenarios specify freshness, data shape, and workload requirements before choosing a store or access path.
chapters.caveat: The video's millions-of-events scaling example is not an unconditional throughput promise. Capacity, ingestion design, query load, and measured latency still matter.

chapters.title: Relational requirements and retention tradeoffs
points: The presenter contrasts Eventhouse with traditional relational modeling, transactional workloads, and some complex multi-table analytical patterns.
A workload may use Eventhouse for events and a different store for SQL-centered dimensional processing. Storage duration should follow business and cost requirements.
chapters.caveat: Do not turn these comparisons into claims that KQL cannot join or that Eventhouse cannot retain long histories. Evaluate the actual operation, correctness contract, and policies rather than a categorical ban.

chapters.title: Querysets, tables, functions, and shortcuts
points: A queryset organizes saved queries; a table stores ingested rows; a function packages reusable query logic; a materialized view maintains an aggregation. The demonstration later makes those differences observable.
A shortcut can expose reference data without ingesting another copy, for example device descriptions used to enrich telemetry.
chapters.caveat: A saved function is not a precomputed result cache. Shortcut references and ingested native tables have different lifecycle and performance properties; access to the source remains relevant.

chapters.title: Retention versus hot cache
points: The video distinguishes how long data is retained from how much recent data is kept in the hot cache. The demo later configures these separately.
The advanced questions require retained older rows to remain accessible while concentrating hot storage on the operational query window.
chapters.caveat: Policy age is ordinarily evaluated from ingestion/extent creation, not a user EventTime field. Retention expiry makes data eligible for deletion, with no precise immediate-deletion guarantee. A hotcache-only query can omit retained cold data.

chapters.title: Materialized aggregation and the unprocessed delta
points: Materialized views maintain aggregation results for repeated analytical queries. The narrated visits example groups counts by date.
The full view query combines its materialized portion with applicable source rows not yet materialized; an explicitly materialized-only access path has a different freshness contract.
chapters.caveat: A materialized view is not an arbitrary persisted SELECT. Supported query shape and aggregation rules apply, and query speed must not be confused with a guarantee that the materialized portion alone contains every latest row.

chapters.title: Backfill and the meaning of effectiveDateTime
points: Without backfill, a new view begins with subsequent ingestions. Backfill includes existing qualifying source records instead.
The cases deliberately supply both EventTime and ingestion time, so eligibility and final time-bucket placement can be reasoned about separately.
chapters.caveat: effectiveDateTime filters ingestion time for backfill, not the event timestamp chosen in the aggregation. Add an explicit event-time predicate to the view query if the business requires one.

chapters.title: Creation syntax, asynchronous work, and readiness
points: The example names the view, its source table, properties, descriptive docString, and the query defining its aggregate.
The rigorous version uses the operation ID to monitor backfill completion before releasing dependent dashboard queries.
chapters.caveat: Correction to the narration: backfill=true requires async, and the view is not available for queries until backfill completes. Transient backfill steps may retry internally; a failed creation operation requires explicit re-execution after remediation. Backfill input must be available in hot cache.

chapters.title: OneLake availability: Delta representation and replication
points: The video enables availability for a database or individual table so Spark and other supported engines can consume Delta without a manually managed export workflow.
Database enablement automatically applies to new tables; existing tables require the Apply to existing tables option when enabling at database scope.
chapters.caveat: This is a managed logical Delta copy, not a promise of zero replication or immediate identical visibility. Adaptive batching can delay OneLake writes; set and monitor the actual freshness requirement.

chapters.title: Retention propagation, restrictions, and the promotion break
points: Retention also applies to the exposed OneLake data. Turning availability off soft deletes that representation; re-enabling includes historic backfill.
The video lists operations requiring a feature-state change, then transitions through a short channel promotion before opening Fabric.
chapters.caveat: Current docs permit adding or deleting columns; column-type changes, table renames, KQL table RLS, and delete/truncate/purge remain restricted while enabled. Disabling a replication feature is not by itself a complete secure-access design.

chapters.title: Eventhouse overview, resources, and endpoints
points: The presenter opens the existing Eventhouse, shows its default database/queryset, overview monitoring, database creation, minimum consumption setting, Python plugins, and query/ingestion URIs.
The demo surveys those controls rather than configuring a production capacity or plugin policy.
chapters.caveat: A URI is an access endpoint, not permission. The overview illustrates management across databases; it does not establish isolation, unlimited throughput, or a completed capacity optimization.

chapters.title: Database ingestion routes, query tools, and policies
points: The menu offers sample/local files, OneLake, Eventstream, Blob/Event Hubs, S3, pipelines/dataflows, and Real-Time Hub routes. Querysets, notebooks, and real-time dashboards are shown as consumption choices.
The demo explains database retention, hot-cache duration, and database-level versus table-level OneLake availability.
chapters.caveat: A connector list is not a substitute for checking source format, authentication, schema mapping, and actual pipeline completion. A hot-cache window changes storage/performance, not the business retention requirement.

chapters.title: Reference data through shortcuts
points: The presenter shows shortcut options from OneLake and external stores and proposes device metadata as reference enrichment for incoming readings.
The quiz adds a join-grain constraint: multiple reference rows per device can multiply telemetry unless one intended reference match is established.
chapters.caveat: No shortcut is actually created in this segment. The lab's reference join examples are original extensions, not a claim that the video demonstrates deduplication or a specific join result.

chapters.title: Table enablement, a Lakehouse shortcut, and Spark access
points: OneLake availability is enabled on the temperature table. In the Lakehouse shortcut dialog, only that enabled table is offered in the demonstrated setup.
The presenter contrasts path-based Delta access in a notebook with reading via the KQL endpoint when the representation is unavailable.
chapters.caveat: The narrated visibility demonstration does not provide a cross-engine zero-latency guarantee. Validate mirroring state and available rows before relying on the replica for a particular report.

chapters.title: Create a visits table and a view without backfill
points: The demo creates a table with visit identity, timestamp, and page, ingests example rows with inline syntax, and inspects them.
A daily-count materialized view is created without backfill. Its initial result is empty because existing ingestions were not included; later source ingestions are included.
chapters.caveat: 'From now on' refers to ingestion eligibility. A late-arriving old event can still contribute to an earlier EventTime bucket after view creation.

chapters.title: Compare backfilled history and later ingestions
points: The second view uses backfill and effectiveDateTime. The narrated old-data example produces daily counts 2, 1, and 2, and its docString appears in the view listing.
Two new rows are then ingested: the no-backfill view contains their fourth-day count of 2, while the backfilled view also retains the earlier aggregates.
chapters.caveat: The exact on-screen KQL was not frame-inspected. Our original case data supplies explicit timestamps and ingestion eligibility rather than assuming the event-time grouping column determines the backfill cutoff.

chapters.title: Parameterized daily visits per page
points: A stored function accepts a page-name parameter, filters the visits table before its daily aggregation, and is invoked separately for homepage and blog.
The narrated blog result has one visit on the third day. The lab extends the pattern into dynamic-value conversions, exact unique-event counts, filtering order, and join cardinality.
chapters.caveat: Reuse of query logic does not mean results are precomputed. Preserve the page and time grain needed by the requested result before choosing where a filter can be applied.

chapters.title: Closing practice, current corrections, and independent scenarios
points: The creator presents two introductory items about backfill/async and OneLake storage after a practice-site promotion, then closes the episode.

This bank uses new scenarios and code, with independent calculations and review. Backfill readiness and schema restrictions are answered according to the current official contract, where the narration is outdated.
chapters.caveat: The complete 776-segment English auto-caption transcript and narrated demos were analyzed. No frame-by-frame visual claim or copied creator practice question is made. A 100-minute topic challenge and raw exact-match score are training settings, not Microsoft's live exam configuration.

chapters.title: Three original cases and independent correctness review
points: The historical-aggregation case separates source ingestion eligibility from the event date reported. The OneLake case checks replica freshness, retention, and access-design constraints. The telemetry case checks deduplication and reference-join grain.

Question authors researched official documentation independently; a separate reviewer checked answer uniqueness, distractors, numeric results, and current feature contracts. Automated interaction checks exercise the final integrated bank and preserved earlier packs.
chapters.caveat: These checks strengthen the practice bank but do not establish psychometric equivalence to Microsoft's undisclosed live questions. Exact KQL execution in a real Fabric workspace and rendered browser QA remain outside the verified checks in this environment.
